questions.question: There are 13 hearts and 12 face cards in a deck. Why is the number of cards that are hearts or face cards 22, not 25?
options: Because face cards are not counted as hearts
Because the jack, queen and king of hearts were counted twice, so we subtract the 3-card overlap
Because the ace of hearts is excluded
Because we must subtract the 4 kings

questions.question: In three-set inclusion-exclusion, after adding |A|+|B|+|C| and subtracting the three pairwise intersections, how many times has an element in all three sets been counted?
options: Twice, so subtract the triple intersection
Zero times, so the triple intersection must be added back
Three times, so subtract it twice
questions.explanation: It is added 3 times (once per set) and subtracted 3 times (once per pair), leaving 0. Adding |A∩B∩C| restores it to exactly 1.

questions.question: Boston has about 650,000 residents and no one has more than 200,000 hairs. What does the generalized pigeonhole principle let you conclude?
options: Someone in Boston has exactly the same number of hairs as you
Every hair count from 1 to 200,000 is shared by at least 3 people
Exactly 4 people share each hair count
At least 4 Bostonians have exactly the same number of hairs
questions.explanation: 650,000 > 3 × 200,000, so some hair count (box) holds at least 3 + 1 = 4 people. The principle says nothing about specific people or about every box.

questions.question: To prove C(n, k) = C(n−1, k−1) + C(n−1, k) by double counting, which split of the binary strings of length n with k ones works?
options: Split by whether the last bit is 1 or 0
Split by whether the first two bits are equal
Split by whether k is even or odd
Split by whether the string is a palindrome
questions.explanation: Ending in 1 leaves k−1 ones in n−1 spots, C(n−1, k−1). Ending in 0 leaves k ones in n−1 spots, C(n−1, k). The cases are disjoint and exhaustive.
